story:
Aurora sat on her front steps with the phone warm in her hands, thumbing through the group chat. Jazlyn had posted a poll about the science fair, and Khadija had already voted for volcanoes twice using two different emoji. Aurora was about to type "volcano, obviously" when the chat buzzed with a new message from Jazlyn: Post a selfie from wherever you are RIGHT NOW. Winner gets bragging rights.

She flipped the camera around. Her hair looked good today, the afternoon light was soft, and the porch swing made a nice background. She took three shots, picked the best one, and her thumb hovered over send. Then she noticed something small in the corner of the photo, pale and square against the door frame. She pinched the screen and zoomed in until it filled half the image. The house number. All four digits, crisp and readable.

Jazlyn sent a photo of her own feet on a bus. Khadija sent one from the library, and behind her shoulder Aurora could just make out the edge of the school logo on a banner. Aurora stared at it while her brain tried to digest what she was seeing. Anybody in the chat could look at Khadija's picture and know which school they went to. Anybody who was not even in the chat, if the photo got shared on, could see it too, because once something was posted it never really went away. And her own picture had the house number in it, which meant anyone could work out exactly where it was taken. Not the town. The house.

She thought about last summer, when she had posted a picture of her new bike leaning against the garage, and a comment had appeared from an account with no profile picture: nice bike. She had deleted it and forgotten it. Now the memory sat uncomfortably, like a stone in a shoe. She couldn't see who had written it. That was the trouble. There was no mechanism for knowing who was watching, or how far a photo travelled, or who saved it to their own phone.

Aurora cropped the picture until only her face and a strip of porch railing remained. "Where's your background?" Khadija typed. "Boring steps," Aurora sent back. Then Jazlyn posted her bus selfie again with a caption, "look closer at the window reflection, you can see my stop." Below it she added, "Uh. Maybe delete that one."

Mr. Menon came up the walk with his dog, raising a hand in greeting. Aurora raised the phone, snapped a picture of just the dog, and sent it with the caption, "safest selfie of the day." The chat filled with laughing emoji as she hit send on the cropped one too.

story:
Muhammad stood on the stage of the community theatre with his note cards sweating in his hand. In three days he had to give a two-minute speech at the youth showcase, and his topic was why people should finish antibiotics they're prescribed instead of stopping when they feel better. He had an opening hook: "Imagine feeling sick and then holding a tiny bottle of medicine in your hand." He had three points, and Ms. Bear had written explicit instructions on the signup sheet: hook, three points, closing. But he had no closing at all.

His friend Jaxon sprawled across a red velvet seat in the front row, scrolling his phone. "Just say 'thank you' at the end," Jaxon offered.

"That's not a closing, that's a fire alarm," Muhammad said. He tried reciting his points, pacing the boards. The speech had a start and a middle and then it just fell off a cliff. He wondered why some speeches felt finished and this one didn't. Was there something invisible, some rule he was missing?

Jaxon held up his phone. "Soraya texted." Muhammad climbed down and read the message: "Stuck on your ending? Look at your first line. When a closing returns to the opening hook at the end, it makes a speech feel complete. My brother calls it a callback. Try it."

Muhammad read the message twice. His hook was about the bottle of medicine. So the ending could come back to it. He walked to centre stage and tried it out loud, recounting his three points, then: "So take the pills until the bottle is empty. Because that tiny bottle isn't holding medicine for today. It's holding medicine for the whole war." He paused, half expecting it to fall flat again, but instead the last line seemed to click into place like a stage flat swinging shut.

"Whoa," said Jaxon. "Do that again."

Muhammad grinned, flipped his cards back to the top, and began, "Imagine feeling sick and then holding a tiny bottle of medicine in your hand."

story:
Matthew sat in the waiting room of Ms. Mercado's studio with his fingertips pressed against the cold metal leg of his chair, because cold felt better than the burning he got whenever he touched his guitar strings. He had been playing for exactly one week, and he was ready to draft his letter of resignation. He'd even worked out the first line: "Dear Guitar, this isn't working out."

"You're quitting?" said Denis, who was waiting for his drum lesson and drumming on the armrest of the couch without using his hands at all, which took real talent. "You practiced like four hours last Saturday."

"That was the problem." Matthew held up his left hand. The tips of his fingers were shiny and red, like little strawberries. "The strings dug grooves in them. I played 'Ode to Joy' nine times and now I can't even feel my locker combination."

The studio door opened and Maisie came out, sliding her own guitar into its case. She was two years ahead of Matthew in lessons and could play a riff that made everyone in the school talent show forget about the magic act. She looked at his hand, and instead of saying something sympathetic, she laughed. Then she held out her own left hand, palm up, and tapped her fingertips.

"Feel those," she said.

They were hard, like the heels of a shoe. "Calluses," she said. "Mine used to hurt too. First month, I almost quit. Then I practiced a little every single day instead of four hours once, and the skin got tough."

"Wait," Matthew said slowly. "So practicing more spread out makes it stop hurting?" He turned this over the way he turned over ideas in class, like the time he'd argued in social studies that a monarchy wasn't automatically obsolete just because it was old, and had actually won the debate. Maybe the same thing applied here. Maybe the problem wasn't the guitar. Maybe the problem was the plan.

That evening he made a chart on graph paper: ten minutes a day, every day, no heroics. By Tuesday his fingers still stung. By Friday they stung less. On Wednesday of the next week, he pressed down a chord and felt the strings push back against something that felt like a thin, hard shield, and he played "Ode to Joy" three times in a row without once wincing.

At his next lesson, he walked into Ms. Mercado's studio, sat down, and laid his left hand on the music stand like evidence.

"Listen to this," he said, and hit a G chord that rang out clean and clear all the way to the sidewalk.

"Already cropping," she said. "I keep records. Deleting is for amateurs."

By evening the cropped version was the one everyone was replying to. Ezra sent a private message: "Old copies are still out there somewhere. Can't un-save what people saved." Tristan read it twice. story:
Evelyn had clicked the little green "Ad" tag on the same search result four times before Fatimah leaned over her shoulder in the computer lab. "Why do you keep doing that?" Fatimah whispered. Evelyn explained her experiment: type "pangolin extinction" into the search bar, count the real results, then count the ads at the top. She wanted to prove she could tell them apart, because Mr. Malik had said it was a crucial skill and she planned to confess in front of the whole class that she couldn't. That was the plan, anyway. The problem was that every time she clicked an ad, it took her to a strange page about "wildlife sponsorships," and she clicked back and clicked it again, testing whether the ad would follow her like a shadow.

"Stop," said Violet from the next station, not even looking up. "That ad's going to keep coming back no matter how many times you poke it."

Evelyn froze with her finger over the mouse. On the whiteboard at the front of the lab, Mr. Malik had written "TODAY: SEARCH LIKE A DETECTIVE," and beside the projector sat his laptop, which was open to a video he had queued for the class. Evelyn could read the title from her seat: an interview with the owner of a small online plant shop. When Mr. Malik finally pressed play, the shop owner held up a potted fern and said, "Advertisers bid in an auction for search keywords, and usually they pay only when someone clicks their ad. It's called pay-per-click."

The room went quiet except for the fan humming in the corner. Evelyn's stomach dropped. Every click. She looked down at her own screen, at the sponsorship ad she had poked four times, and did the math fast: someone, somewhere, had just paid for four clicks from a girl who wanted a pangolin. She wasn't testing the ad. She was spending a stranger's money.

She raised her hand. "Mr. Malik, I have to confess something before we start."

He paused the video and raised an eyebrow.

Evelyn dragged her chair aside so the whole class could see her screen. "I found out how ads work. The expensive way."

story:
Paige pushed a piece of broccoli around her plate and pretended to chew. Tomorrow was the semifinal, and she was the backup goalie, which meant she might stand in the net for the whole game or for none of it, and her stomach could not decide which one was worse.

"You're quiet," her mother said, spooning rice into her bowl. "Bad day?"

"Not bad exactly." Paige set down her fork. "Emaan says I'll probably have to face at least one penalty shot. She's the regular keeper, and she told me her secret. Before a penalty shot, she breathes out slowly, longer than she breathes in. She says it settles her body down so the stress doesn't take over." She glanced up. "Is that a real thing or just a goalie thing?"

"It's a real thing," her mother said. "Slow breathing with a long exhale is a coping skill. People use it on purpose, right before a stressful moment, because it calms the body's stress response. I do it before big meetings." She smiled a little. "I used it today before I told my boss I needed better boundaries around weekend emails. That word means lines you set so people know what you'll accept. My hands were shaking and my anxiety was doing cartwheels, but I breathed out slow, and it helped."

Paige looked at her plate. In science class, Ms. He had taught them that you couldn't just believe a claim, you had to replicate it, which meant trying the same thing yourself and seeing if you got the same result. Devyn had replicated the herbivore experiment with two mealworms and a pile of leaves, and it had worked. Maybe a goalie's trick could work the same way. She sat up straight, breathed in through her nose, and let the air out slowly, counting to eight while her mother kept talking about Saturday plans.

The tight feeling in her stomach didn't vanish, but it loosened, like a knot someone had worked a finger into. She tried it again, this time while imagining the ball on the penalty spot, the whole gym silent. In, then out, long and slow. Her shoulders dropped an inch.

"Feeling better?" her mother asked.

"I think I replicated Emaan's experiment," Paige said. She picked up the brittle cracker from the side of her plate, snapped off a corner, and ate it. "And it worked. Tomorrow, before that penalty shot, everybody's going to wonder why the goalie looks like she's just smelling the flowers."

story:
Charlie knocked on Griffin's door three times before anyone answered. Griffin's mom opened it a crack and said he was in his room, but she lowered her voice when she said it, the way people talk about someone sleeping.

Griffin was not sleeping. He sat on his floor with his back against the bed, a half-built robot on his knees. "Hey," he said, and then nothing else. His hands moved the screwdriver in tiny circles without actually turning any screws.

Charlie sat down across from him. She had been building a theory all the way over, because Griffin had skipped lunch twice this week and had not laughed at Heinrich's joke on Friday, which never happened. "Is it the competition?" she asked. Griffin's robotics team had won the regional championship in the fall, a big prestigious tournament, and everyone expected them to go to state. "Everyone keeps asking if we'll win again," Griffin said. "Heinrich keeps grabbing my controller to show me stuff. I keep telling him no and he does it anyway." He set the screwdriver down. "I can't sleep. My stomach hurts before school."

Charlie remembered the poster outside Mr. Ngo's health classroom, the one she had read while waiting for the water fountain in September. Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. She had stood there thinking it was strange that "social" was on the list, right next to emotional, like friends were part of the same system as feelings. At the time it had seemed like a poster fact. Now it seemed like a clue. If social counted, then Heinrich grabbing the controller was not just annoying. It was part of what was making Griffin sick, the same way lost sleep was.

"I made an assumption," Charlie said. "I thought you were just stressed about winning. But it's more than that." She picked up the robot and turned it over. "Heinrich keeps violating your boundaries. You said no and he does it anyway. That's not a small thing."

Griffin looked at the robot in her hands. "I didn't know you could call it that. I thought it meant I was being dramatic."

"You're not being dramatic. Stress is a real thing, anxiety is a real thing, and there are ways of coping with them, and one way is telling the person causing it to knock it off." Charlie handed the robot back. "Want me to text Heinrich?"

Griffin pulled out his phone himself and typed while Charlie watched. He held the screen up so she could read it: "You keep taking my controller after I say no. Stop. I mean it."

"Send it," Charlie said. He did.

Ethan set the pizza dough bowl on the picnic table and glared at it, because the last two batches had come out of the grill oven dry and cakey, more like biscuits than bread. Markus leaned over the fence from next door, and Ethan felt a stab of envy at the perfect-looking bun Markus was eating. "Your dough still sad?" Markus asked. "It's a paradox," Ethan said. "Follow the recipe exactly, get exactly the wrong thing." Ryder arrived on his bike just then, skidding to a stop on the grass. "You can't follow a recipe exactly," he said. "Nobody can."

That was the problem, Ethan realized. He had been measuring the flour by dipping the cup straight into the bag, the way you'd scoop sand at the beach. His grandma had shown him once, spooning flour gently into the cup and leveling it off with a knife, but he'd thought it was just her being fussy about tidiness. Now he wondered if there was a real difference. So he tried an experiment right there at the picnic table. He scooped a cup of flour straight from the bag, dumped it onto the scale, and wrote the number down. Then he spooned flour into the same cup, leveled it, and weighed that too. The scooped cup was heavier, a lot heavier. Same cup, same flour, two different amounts.

"So the recipe thinks a cup is one thing, and your cup is another," Markus said slowly, watching the numbers. Ethan nodded. "Scooping packs the flour down. Weighing it is more accurate than any cup." He was quiet for a second, then said in his most assertive voice, "New rule. Nobody scoops in this backyard." Ryder raised his hand. "What if it's ice cream?" "Ice cream is exempt."

Ethan weighed out the flour for a fresh batch, kneaded it until it felt like an earlobe, which his grandma said was the goal, and slid the dough into a bowl to rise in the sun. When he punched it down an hour later and it sprang back soft and smooth, he whooped so loudly that Markus dropped his bun over the fence. "Dinner's at six!" Ethan called. "Bring your appetite, not your scooping hand."

story:
Carter stood in the kitchen holding six index cards and a kitchen timer, and he said, for the fourth time, "Today I will talk about bees." His dad looked up from chopping an onion and nodded politely. His little sister kept drawing her dinosaur. Carter stopped. He had a two-minute speech due in Ms. Hoang's class on Friday, and it was supposed to have an opening hook, three points and a closing, and so far every practice run had made his family act like furniture.

He tried again in the living room that evening. "Today I will talk about sharks." His dad flipped a page of his magazine without reading it, Carter was almost sure. That was the strange part. His dad liked sharks. So why did everyone's attention drift away the second Carter began? He sat on the arm of the couch and wondered about it. It was like the audience's focus could fluctuate, rising and falling depending on something Carter couldn't see, some rule hiding underneath the words themselves.

On Saturday his friend Charles-Edouard came over, and they watched old speeches on a tablet. One kid started with "Today I will talk about recycling," and Carter felt his own eyes go fuzzy. The next video opened with "Did you know a single beehive can hold fifty thousand bees?" and Carter sat up without meaning to. He rewound it. He watched three more videos, keeping a tally on a napkin, and a pattern appeared. The speeches that grabbed him began with a question, a surprising fact, or a very short story. The boring ones began with an announcement.

"See, it's the first line," Carter said. "It's called a hook. A question, or a weird fact, or a tiny story."

Charles-Edouard frowned. "So it isn't about the topic at all?"

"It's about the opening." Carter grabbed a fresh card. He wrote three hooks for his bee speech: a question, a fact, and a thirty-second story about the time a bee followed him around the backyard for a whole afternoon like a tiny buzzing protagonist. Then he decided to test it, because a pattern on a napkin wasn't proof. Sunday dinner, his whole family at the table, was his laboratory.

He cleared his throat. "Which is smarter, a bee or a pigeon?" The conversation stopped. His sister put down her fork. "A bee," his dad said, "surely." "Wrong," said Carter, and launched into his first point. His sister interrupted twice to argue, which was rude but also, Carter thought, exactly the point. Nobody picked up a phone. Nobody drifted. He finished with his closing line, checked the timer, and grinned. Monday at recess he found Finlay by the fence.

"Hey, Finlay. Want to hear the smartest insect in the world?"

Mila stood at the front of the drama camp's black-box studio, notes shaking in her hand, and began her two-minute speech about why her school should keep its bee garden. "Um, honeybees visit, um, two million flowers just to make one pound of honey," she said. From the front row, Zayden clicked a tally counter with every "um," and by the end of the first run-through it read thirty-one.

Thirty-one felt terrible, but Mila noticed something while she watched the playback on Ms. Friedman's tablet. When she paused silently before her second point, Zayden leaned forward. When she said "um," he glanced at the ceiling. She wondered if the filler words were the problem rather than the nerves underneath, and she had a way to test it. "Count again," she told Zayden, "but this time clap when I pause instead of counting ums."

The second run had fewer than half the ums, because every time she felt one coming, she shut her mouth and let the quiet sit there. The pauses felt enormous to her, like falling, but Zayden clapped twelve times and only sixteen tally marks appeared. Jared, who was writing the closing line of his own speech, looked up and said, "You sound way more confident when you stop like that. It gives me a second to actually take in the point." That matched what Mila had seen on the playback, and she wrote "PAUSE" in red letters at the top of each of her three points.

The camp showcase came on Friday, with parents folding themselves into the small chairs. Mila's opening hook about the two million flowers landed, and when she reached her second point she paused, one second of silence in a room that had been noisy all morning. Nobody fidgeted. Her closing line, "The bees did the work; the least we can do is keep the garden," got a real laugh and then applause.

Afterward Zayden held up the tally counter, which read four. "Four, and two of those were borderline," he said. Mila grinned and tossed her notes into her bag, because even the protagonist of a bee speech deserves a break, and trivial mistakes were just data now. "Same time tomorrow?" Jared asked, waving his still-unfinished closing line at her. "Bring the counter," Mila said.

story:
Jaxson's whole week had started to revolve around the science project on Ms. Sánchez's back table: a battery, a bulb, a switch, and three wires that were supposed to make light. Yesterday it had worked. The bulb had glowed like a tiny sun every time he flipped the switch, and Tristen had clapped so loudly that a kid two rooms over probably heard it. Today, on demo day, he flipped the switch and nothing happened. The bulb sat there, dark and smug, like it was keeping a secret.

"Maybe the bulb died of boredom," Tristen said, leaning over Jaxson's shoulder. The table smelled like pencil shavings and the orange peel somebody had left there since Monday.

"It worked yesterday," Jaxson said. "That's the part that's making me crazy." He wiggled each wire where it clamped to the battery. He unscrewed the bulb and screwed it back. He clicked the switch up, down, up, down, and even held it halfway, which Finley said was like standing in the median between on and off. Still dark. Finley offered a replacement bulb from her kit, and the whole class watched, because whether Jaxson's project could be fixed had somehow become the most controversial question of the morning, bigger even than whether cafeteria pizza counted as breakfast.

Then Jaxson stopped moving his hands and thought. Something invisible had to be the problem, because everything he could see looked fine. A circuit was a loop, and the loop only lit the bulb if something was flowing through it. What if the thing flowing had stopped, not because of a broken wire, but because the battery itself had run out? Yesterday he had left the switch on by accident, all afternoon and all night. The battery could have been slowly using itself up the whole time. "Tristen," he said slowly, "hand me the battery out of Finley's kit."

He swapped it in, pressed the wires tight, and flipped the switch. The bulb blazed. The class actually cheered, and Ms. Sánchez raised both eyebrows like she'd won something.

"So what happened?" she asked.

"The battery turns its stored chemical energy into electrical energy," Jaxson said, holding the old battery up like evidence in a trial, "and when those chemicals get used up, it goes flat. Mine went flat, because I left my switch on overnight and drained it." He turned the dead battery over in his fingers and grinned. "This little guy worked himself to the bone."

"Rest in peace," Tristen said, saluting the battery.

Jaxson dropped it in the paper cup marked "dead batteries" and flipped his switch off, very, very deliberately.

Addison slid her story across the desk to Kendra, who read fast and then frowned. "You only fixed the spelling. Mr. Virtanen said we have to revise."

"That is revising," Addison said. "New commas and everything."

Kendra, who wanted the reading corner spot by the window and knew Mr. Virtanen gave it to whoever improved the most, shook her head. "No. He told Liana the word revise comes from the Latin revisere, meaning 'to look at again.' Revising means seeing your draft with fresh eyes."

Addison looked at her page again. All she saw was the same page. She tried standing up, walking once around the desks, and coming back. That was no better. Then she had an idea: if her eyes were the problem, maybe her ears were the answer. She read the first paragraph out loud in a low voice.

"Leila walked slowly and quietly through the very dark and spooky old hallway." It sounded flat, like a hallway itself. She crossed out slowly and quietly and wrote crept. She crossed out very dark and spooky old and kept only the shadowed hallway. Then she noticed something else. Every sentence was long. Every single one had two commas in it. She cut one sentence down to four words: "The floor creaked. She froze."

Her pencil wanted to rebel against deleting words she had worked hard on, but she reminded herself she was being frugal, keeping only what the paragraph truly needed. Reading aloud took stamina, because she kept stopping to slash adjectives, but by the end she had crossed out eleven of them.

She read it to Kendra again. "The floor creaked. She froze." Kendra grinned and pointed at the last line.

"Read that part one more time," Kendra said.

The bus was leaving the historic site at two thirty, sharp, and Ms. Ngo had already promised that anyone left behind would become "part of the exhibit." Dylan took this as a personal challenge, not because he wanted to stay, but because the old farmhouse had one thing he could not stop staring at: a writing desk in the corner with a dark, shiny patch worn right into the wood.

He drifted toward it while the guide talked about candle molds. His fingers were halfway to the patch when Jagger grabbed his sleeve like a lifeguard. "Whoa. You can't touch that. Ms. Ngo said. The oils and salts from your skin build up over time and stain the wood, or damage the surface. That's why they put ropes around everything."

Dylan pulled his hand back and stared at the dark patch again. Something clicked. "Wait. If skin oils build up over time and stain the surface, then that patch is like a fingerprint collection. Hundreds of hands. Maybe the family counted their money there, or wrote letters, or did homework, even." Victor wandered over, chewing the strap of his backpack. "That's not a credible theory. It's a desk. Desks get used. Case closed, detective."

"It's not just used," Dylan said. "The stain has a shape. Look, it's not everywhere, it's in one band along the front edge. That's an anomaly, Victor. It means people stood on one side, over and over, for years." Victor squinted at the desk, then at the window beside it. "Okay, or the sun hits it there." Dylan considered that, then shook his head. "Sun fades wood. This is darker. And shinier."

The guide was already moving the group toward the kitchen, and the clock on the mantel said 2:15, which meant fifteen minutes before the bus became a memory and they became history. Dylan raised his hand like he was launching it off his wrist. "Can you cite any record of who used the desk? Like letters or inventories?"

The guide blinked, then smiled. "As a matter of fact, yes. The middle daughter ran the farm's accounts from that desk for forty years. Standing at the front edge, where the light from this window fell on her ledger."

"Ha!" Dylan spun around to Victor and Jagger, pointing at the dark band of forty years of ledger-keeping. "Standing. Front edge. I told you."

"You got lucky," Victor said, but he was grinning.

"Excuse me," the guide added, "I'd ask you not to high-five next to the desk."

Dylan and Jagger froze, palms hovering in the air, and backed away to the sound of the whole class laughing at them.

Archie read. "Nothing's wrong with it. It's good."

"See, that's the problem. You can't see anything in it." She tapped the page. "My whole field trip essay is 'nice' and 'interesting' and 'good.' My grandmother read it last night and asked me what exactly was nice about the trip. I said, you know, nice. She said the word gives my opinion without showing anything, and a concrete detail lets the reader picture it and judge."

"That sounds like something a grandmother would enforce at dinner," Archie said.

"She did. She wouldn't pass the potatoes until I answered."

Lily picked up her pencil and read her opening sentence aloud, quietly, because Mr. Bekele was reshelving books two rows over and his rule about voices was the one rule he actually enforced. "The science museum was very interesting." She crossed out "very interesting." Now she had "The science museum was." She stared at it.

Himmat dropped into the third chair with his backpack, which was, as always, perpendicular to the table instead of under it, so everyone had to step around him. "What are we doing?"

"Concrete details," Lily said. "Apparently 'good' and 'interesting' are words you write when you haven't decided what actually happened."

Himmat looked wounded. "I use those words."

"You do. Your volcano essay said the demonstration generator was 'cool.' Was it loud? Did it spark? Did it smell like burnt toast? Cool tells me nothing except that you liked it."

"It did smell like burnt toast," Himmat admitted. "The whole lab did."

Lily wrote that down. Then she kept going, testing each sentence the way her grandmother had tested her: if the word only gave her opinion, out it came. The giant turbine became a wheel taller than Mr. Bekele. The good exhibit became the one where you cranked a handle and a light bulb glowed faintly, then died, then glowed again. The nice bus ride home became thirty-seven minutes of Archie humming one song without stopping.

"I heard that," Archie said, not looking up.

"You were meant to." She read her new opening under her breath: sentences short, then long, then short again, like her grandmother's own storytelling, which never used the same rhythm twice in a row. She turned the page around and slid it back across the table. "Now tell me what's wrong with it."

Archie read. "Nothing's wrong with it. It's good."

Lily raised her pencil. "Try that again with a detail."

Umar was already inside, holding his phone out like a waiter's tray. "Logan, look. What he didn't know was which direction that was from here, in this hall, on this rainy Tuesday.

"I thought the wall with the designs was the front," Logan said. Mathieu, who had come along because his own family was busy and he wanted to see what a mosque was like, pointed at the geometric tiles. "Then why does your app point at the coat rack?"

He turned ninety degrees, and the line swung behind him. He turned back, and it locked onto the windows again. So the tiles were pretty, and the tiles were not the point. The point was Mecca, wherever Mecca happened to be. "The front isn't where the designs are," he said slowly. "The front is toward the Kaaba."

Ms. Grewal, who ran the community lunch and had been stacking paper cups, set the cups down and came to look. "You've got it," she said, and nothing more, which made Logan feel oddly proud, as if he'd solved it himself instead of an app solving it for him. "So," Mathieu said as they rolled up the mat, "does Umar's phone have a monopoly on compasses, or can I try it too?" Eleanor sat at the kitchen computer with her science worksheet beside the keyboard. One question was underlined twice: Is the claim "houseplants improve focus" backed by tested evidence, or is it only a story about one person's experience? She typed the claim into the search box and got a blog post first, written by a woman who said three ferns on her desk had changed her life. The post was funny and easy to read, and Eleanor almost copied the address onto her worksheet.

Then she noticed the second result, an article in something called a journal. It was harder to read, full of words like "participants" and "controlled conditions," and it described an experiment with fifty students, half of them seated near plants and half not. She scrolled down both pages side by side. The blog was one person's bizarre, wonderful luck with ferns. The journal article documented its results in tables, and at the bottom it said the article had been reviewed before publication. Reviewed by whom, Eleanor wondered, and why did that matter?

She called Jordynn, who had finished the worksheet the night before. "Did your article say anything about being checked?" Eleanor asked. "Mine says it was reviewed." There was a rustling on the other end, then Jordynn's voice, pleased with herself. "That's peer review. "So the blog lady's ferns," she said slowly, "nobody checked those." "Right," said Jordynn. "She's just telling you what happened to her. That's a story about one person's experience, not tested evidence."

Eleanor looked at the two windows on the screen. If she used the blog, her worksheet would take five minutes, but the answer would be wobbly, and the consequence might be a red mark from Mr. Henry, who liked sources. The journal article had taken her twenty minutes to puzzle through, but fifty students beat three ferns, and experts had combed it for mistakes first. She clicked print on the journal page, picked the warm sheets off the printer, and wrote her answer in her best handwriting. Then she set a small pothos cutting beside the monitor, just in case the fern lady had been onto something anyway.

On Saturday mornings Landon worked at Ms. Ross's farm stand, stacking baskets of strawberries and trying not to eat the evidence. At noon the strawberries were four dollars a basket. At five o'clock, right before closing, Ms. Ross marched out and turned the sign to one dollar. Landon stared at it. "That's backwards. Everyone loves strawberries. Shouldn't popular things cost more?"

Sabrina, who was sweeping between the pie table and the cooler, leaned on her broom. "It's supply and demand," she said. "We learned it Tuesday."

"A contradiction, that's what it is," said Landon. "More people wanting them should mean more money, not less. Unless you're hiding something, like a strawberry thief."

"Feel the flat," Ms. Ross said, dumping a crate of unsold baskets into his arms. The cardboard was porous and already going soft where the juice had touched it, and under the green smell of the berries there was a faint edge of something sweeter, something almost wrong.

Landon turned a basket over in his hands and did the math out loud. "These were picked yesterday. They can't just sit around. Fresh strawberries spoil within days of picking, so if you have too many, you can't store them for later. You have to cut the price to sell them now, or they're garbage by Tuesday."

"Garbage by Monday, actually," said Ms. Ross, "but you've got the idea."

"So the price isn't about how much people want them," Landon said slowly. "It's about the clock." He adjusted the sign so the big one-dollar side faced the road, and within ten minutes three cars pulled in.

Sabrina counted the last basket into a woman's bag. "Supply and demand," she said smugly, "and the demand of strawberries to become compost."

"Mine's about water temperature," Kaylee said, unpacking her watering bottles. "Cold versus room temperature, everything else the same." She held up a small brass valve she'd borrowed from her dad's garage. "This controls the drip so both pots get exactly the same amount. I have to keep it durable enough to survive three kids bumping the table."

Jean wasn't listening. She was staring at her plants, and one was tall and leaning while the other was short and straight. "They were identical," she said. "Same music, same soil, same water. I even measured. But the tall one only got tall this week, and I don't know why."

Kaylee crouched down to look. The tall plant was stretched sideways, reaching, its leaves turned one direction. She turned the pot slowly, then turned back. "Which one sat closer to the window?"

Jean looked up at the tall windows above the bleachers, then at her table. "The leaning one. It's been in that spot since Tuesday. I moved the whole setup to make room for Tyler's volcano."

"So it's not the music," Kaylee said. "In a fair test, every other condition has to stay the same, so any difference in results can be traced to the one thing you changed." She said it slowly, checking it against her own experiment as the words came out. "Your one thing was supposed to be music. But sunlight snuck in there too, so now you can't tell what caused what."

Jean groaned and put her head in her arms. "The fair opens in forty minutes."

"Then swap them," Kaylee said. "Put both pots the same distance from the window, equal light on both sides, and start your counts over. Or, wait." Kaylee pointed at the other side of Jean's sign, which had room left. "You could keep the old data and elaborate on it. Write down what went wrong. Judges like it when you show how you caught a mistake."

Jean sat up. "Really? Not just crossed out and redone?"

"Mine almost fell apart twice," Kaylee said. "The valve dripped unevenly for two days before I caught it. I logged that too." She handed Jean a fresh index card and her own marker. "Here. Start with the window."

Tyler wandered over from his volcano, wiping baking soda off his hands, and read Jean's card while Jean wrote. "So the plant wasn't reaching toward the music," he said. "It was reaching toward the light."

"Exactly one variable," Jean said, and underlined the last line of her card.

By the time Mr. Cohen came around with his clipboard, Jean's table held two evenly lit pots, a drip valve borrowed from Kaylee's kit, and a sign that read, in fresh marker: A fair test keeps every other condition the same. The tall plant still leaned toward the window, stubborn and green, like it was pointing at the answer.

"I'm strengthening it," Kate said. "Flour has proteins in it, and when they mix with water, something called gluten forms. Kneading makes the gluten stronger and stretchier." She held up both pieces. She covered the bowl with a towel and left it in the sun. Her grandmother had never gotten to taste the loaf they started together; that choice, to wander off instead of staying, sat with Kate while the dough rose and puffed under the towel. Maybe the old dense loaf had been her fault, maybe not. When she peeled the towel back an hour later, the dough had swelled round and proud, and she carried the bowl inside to the oven, calling over her shoulder, "Mr. Cho, come back at dinner. "That sounds like a rule," Adrian said. "Rules need a name."

"The jury's still out on the name," Lucy said, and he laughed so hard a man at the coffee station turned around. The cashier leaned toward them. "There's a name," she said. "Law of demand." She tapped the sign. "Consistent as sunrise."

Lucy bought one bottle instead of three, and Adrian, instead of sulking, spent his money on her second-choice, a jug of juice that had stayed cheap because nobody wanted it. At the door she paused. "You intervened in the hot chocolate crisis and saved the day," she said, holding up the juice.

Joshua glanced at Mayar, who shrugged and kept arranging the vine. "We'd play music for a plant," Joshua said.

"Any plant? Any music? And what would you expect to see?" Mr. Aziz picked up a bean seedling in a paper cup, turned it toward the window, and set it back down. "Try again Thursday." Then he moved on to torment Calvin, whose volcano had sprung a leak.

Joshua took the bean seedlings home, along with three more cups from the supply shelf that Mr. Aziz let him borrow. He lined up four seedlings on his windowsill and thought about the question all through dinner. What would count as a plant "liking" something? He couldn't ask it. He couldn't see liking. The next morning he wrote his idea on an index card. In class, he slid it across the table to Mayar. "If I play music for two seedlings and keep two seedlings quiet," he read aloud, "then the music seedlings will grow taller by Friday." Mayar leaned in. "That's a hypothesis," she said, pointing at his card. "Mr. Aziz mentioned that word yesterday, remember? It's a guess you can actually test."

So they tested it. Calvin donated his phone as the music source, since his volcano was already ruined anyway. Two cups went behind a cardboard box where the phone played soft piano for an hour each morning. Two cups sat in silence on the other side of the sill. Every day, Joshua measured with a ruler and logged the numbers, and Mayar drew a chart with a line for each plant.

By Friday, the numbers told them something unexpected. The quiet seedlings had grown taller, by half a centimeter, and one music seedling had barely grown at all. "So our hypothesis was wrong," Joshua said slowly, writing the results down anyway.

"Then the poster's wrong too," Mayar said, peeling off the glittery letters. Calvin grinned. "Can we write 'plants might not like music' in giant letters instead?"

"Hypothesis overturned," Joshua said, and uncapped the marker.

Eva typed number = input("Pick a number: ") and then print('7' * 3), because she wanted to test what a loop's inner line would do before she built the whole thing. "Your times table thinks seven times three is seven hundred and seventy-seven," he said, and Mika leaned over to see.

Eva stared at the three sevens marching across the monitor. So multiplying text by a whole number repeats the text, she realized, instead of doing any math at all. The quotes were the clue. She had put quotation marks around the seven, so Python thought she was printing a word made of one character, and '7' * 3 gave '777'. Last month she had done the same kind of thing and quit in frustration, deleting a whole project because she assumed the program was broken. That memory sat with her now, the way the computer lab always sat cold in November because its walls had almost no insulation, so everyone coded in jackets. She had regretted deleting that project for weeks. This time she kept going.

She retrieved her draft from the saved file, found the line with the quotes, and took them away. Then she wrote the loop: for i in range(1, 13): print(number, "times", i, "is", number * i). She pressed run and typed 7.

The table marched down the screen, seven times one is 7, seven times two is 14, all the way to seven times twelve is 84. Mika slid her chair over. "Do nine," she said. "Nines are the weird ones."

Eva cleared the input and typed 9, and while the table scrolled she thought again about the project she had thrown away, and whether next time something looked wrong she would stay or leave. The cursor blinked in the empty input box, waiting.

"Try twelve," Kohen said.

Ms. Gallagher walked past, studied the drawings, and announced that the three of them were hereby founding the gallery's first Anchor Guild, membership requiring one perfectly grounded sphere. "What does the ring symbolize?" Gwen asked, pointing at the dark spot. Naomy grinned. "Gravity," she said, "in pencil form." Gabrielle set her phone face down next to her plate, which was a rule at the dinner table, but she couldn't stop thinking about what was on the screen. Tomorrow morning was the deadline for the school newspaper, and she had half an article written about Friday's soccer match against Lakeside. Then Aspen had texted her a screenshot that said Lakeside's coach had been suspended for cheating and the whole team might be disqualified.

"Two more bites of rice and then you can be excused," her dad said, passing her the chicken.

She ate, chewing fast, and turned the screenshot over in her mind. The post came from somebody on the Northview side, the school Lakeside had beaten last week. It was from a friend of a friend, no name, no source. But Northview kids hated Lakeside right now, so of course they'd share it.

"Can I ask something weird?" she said. "If you already think a team is bad, and somebody tells you the team cheated, do you check it?"

Her mom tilted her head. "Usually not. People grab anything that fits what they already believe and doubt anything that doesn't. Your aunt calls that confirmation bias."

Gabrielle rolled the phrase around. It fit what she was watching herself do. She had read the screenshot and instantly believed it, because Lakeside winning had stung, and the story made the sting make sense. If the post had said Lakeside's players volunteered at a shelter all weekend, she would have demanded three sources.

The deadline ticked closer with every minute. She imagined printing the rumor and then watching Lakeside show up Friday, coach and all, to play the game. The whole article would sit on a foundation that wasn't there. Worse, a rumor like that could spread until it sustained itself, passed along by every Northview kid who wanted it to be true, without anyone checking a single fact.

She picked up her phone, opened her messages, and typed to Aspen: Did anyone actually confirm the suspension? Call the athletic office?

Aspen replied with a shrugging emoji, then: my mom works near the district office, I'll ask.

Gabrielle finished her rice while she waited, watching the screen instead of the plate. A message finally buzzed through. "No suspension on record. Coach is running practice right now, Aspen saw the lights from the parking lot."

"Good news or bad news?" her dad asked.

"Good news for my article." She was already deleting the paragraph, fingers moving fast. "I get to write about how a rumor spread through two schools in one afternoon."

Then she typed a new headline: HOW A FAKE STORY RAN FASTER THAN THE TRUTH.

The snow had come in the night, and by morning school was cancelled, which meant the whole day stretched ahead like the hill behind Eve's house. She pulled on her boots, grabbed the red saucer sled, and met Sydney and Caitlin at the top of the slope, where the pines stood with their branches bowed under the weight of fresh snow.

Eve was halfway through her first run when she noticed something odd. Every time she crashed into the powder at the bottom, the snow flew up in a glittering cloud, and the flakes seemed to hang in the air long enough to be seen. She held out her dark wool mitten, caught one, and looked closely. Six arms, thin as eyelashes, branching out from a tiny center. She caught another. Six arms again. A third flake, lopsided where it had half melted, still showed six.

"Sydney, come look," she called. "I think they all have six."

Sydney tramped over and held out her own mitten, which was navy blue and porous enough that the flakes sank into it and vanished. "Mine keeps eating them," she complained, so she borrowed Eve's. Caitlin nominated herself as record keeper and pulled off a glove to write tallies in the snow with one finger.

They caught flakes for a long while, sledding between rounds, and every single one came out with six. Eve thought about the ones she had seen in picture books and on window screens, and realized she could not remember ever counting one with five, or seven, or eight. "It's like there's a rule," she said. "Snowflakes almost always have six sides or six arms. It must be something about how the water freezes."

"So a five-armed one is impossible?" Caitlin asked, still scratching tallies.

"Almost," said Eve. "That's why I want to keep checking."

Then Sydney shouted so loudly that a crow lifted off the fence post. On her mitten sat a fat, ragged flake that looked like a star that had lost a point. "Seven!" Sydney yelled. "I nominate this one to break the rule!"

Eve leaned in until her breath almost touched it. The flake had two centers, she saw, two little hearts pressed together, with arms overlapping where they had collided on the way down. Each half, when she traced it with her eye, had six arms of its own.

"It's two stuck together," she said. "A snowflake alliance."

Caitlin added two tallies to the snow and looked up, grinning. "Then the rule holds. Now somebody race me to the bottom."

The shovel leaned against the fence post like it had been there all summer, and maybe it had. Andrew set the rusty shovel beside the spade and crouched down to compare them. "I think it's chemical," Andrew said slowly. "Like burning, but slow. The iron with the water and the air, it makes a new thing. It's called iron oxide." He'd found the words in his notebook at the bottom of his backpack, half-copied from the board.

"Is that a fact," said his grandpa, which was not really a question.

Andrew carried the shovel to the fence and laid it flat where he could keep an eye on it. The group chat had been going all afternoon, mostly about the weekend hike Ms. Lee's class was taking to the plateau above the river. Mia was halfway through packing trail mix when her phone buzzed.

Are you mad at me?

It was Macy, in a private message, not the group chat. Mia blinked at it. She scrolled back up. The last thing she had sent Macy was one word: Okay. Except she had typed it "Okay." with a period, the way her thumb automatically did after every sentence.

"I'm not mad," she said out loud to her empty room, then typed, why would I be mad? and hit send with no period at all. Macy replied with a single thumbs-up, which somehow looked even angrier, and Mia flopped backward onto her bed. Something was going on that she could not see, some invisible rule about the messages themselves, and she meant to find it.

She scrolled through their whole conversation, looking for patterns. Messages that ended in periods: "Fine." "Sure." "Okay." Every one of those had started a small argument. Messages with no punctuation, like "haha okay" or "omg yes," always got a happy reply. She remembered last month, when Macy had sent "See you tomorrow." and Mia had spent an hour wondering what she'd done wrong. It worked both ways, apparently. A period at the end of a short text made it feel like Macy was closing a door.

The next morning, Mia brought it up on the way to class. "Marcus, if I text you 'okay,' is that friendly?"

"Obviously," Marcus said. "If you text me 'okay' with a period, you sound like you're firing me from a job."

"That's a real thing, you know," Macy said, catching up to them in the hallway. "My cousin told me about it. In 2016, researchers at Binghamton University found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one." She shrugged. "So it's not just me being weird."

"You looked it up?" Mia asked.

"Last night, after I thought you were mad. I wanted proof before I apologized for something that wasn't even happening." Macy pulled out her phone and showed them the article, and the three of them stood there in the crowded hallway reading it while somebody's trumpet case bumped past.

Marcus wants the group chat to keep planning the hike, and he wants Mia to accompany him on the steep trail because he's scared of heights and won't admit it. "So we're all good?" he asked.

"We're good," Mia said. Then, feeling resilient after a night of worrying, she typed into the group chat: okay no periods ever again, deal?

Three thumbs-ups came back within ten seconds, and one of them, she noticed, had a period after it.

Oliver knelt in the grass beside the pond at Mr. Ross's farm, pencil in hand, drawing his food chain on the back of a permission slip. He started with the frog, then an arrow to the snake, then an arrow to the hawk, because that was the order he'd thought of first.

She held out a note she'd written during the bus ride, a message she'd been saving to tease him with: "Your chain starts with a frog. Frogs don't make food out of nothing. Where does the frog's energy really come from?" Oliver read it twice and frowned. He remembered, suddenly, the pond's green scum from last summer, before the drought. He'd skipped rocks across it while Kallie warned him not to. Now he noticed the same green film edging the shallows, thick along the sunny side and thin in the shade of the willow.

"The sun," he said slowly. He erased the frog, drew a sun instead, and put the arrow from the sun to the algae. "Most food chains start with the sun. Plants and algae, the producers, use sunlight to make their own food by photosynthesis. Then everything that consumes them, the tadpoles, the frogs, the snakes, the hawk, is just passing that energy along." He added the arrows one at a time, sun to algae, algae to tadpole, tadpole to frog.

Chantelle, who had been sampling cheese at the artisan stall near the barn, wandered over with a napkin still in her hand. "So what happens if the algae goes?" she asked. Oliver tested it with his thumb, covering the algae. The chain broke in half. "Everything after it goes hungry. The tadpoles starve, then the frogs, then the hawk. The top predator loses too, even though it never ate algae in its life." He thought about skipping those rocks last summer, how little he'd wondered about any of it. He drew the sun bigger, then wrote his name at the top of the page.

"Alright," said Mr. Ross from the fence, "bring your chains up to the barn."
